html:
Circuit analysis, structural frames, the Google PageRank vector and the normal equations of Unit 2 all lead to systems of linear equations Ax = b, sometimes with thousands of unknowns.

This unit covers direct methods (Gauss elimination, Gauss–Jordan, LU), iterative methods (Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel), the dangers of ill-conditioning, and the power method for eigenvalues.

What this unit gives you
  • Gauss elimination with partial pivoting, Gauss–Jordan inversion, LU factorisation.
  • Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel iteration; convergence and diagonal dominance.
  • Ill-conditioning and the condition number.
  • Eigenvalue estimation by the power method.

Syllabus note. The mirror of the TU CACS252 outline used for this book (see bca/SOURCES.md) lists Units 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 but mentions "Linear Algebraic Equations" in the course description and lab list.

The unit is included here as Unit 4, as in other TU outlines; its 10 hours are the remainder of 45.

4.1 Gauss elimination

Forward elimination converts Ax = b to an upper-triangular system by subtracting multiples m_{ik} = \frac{a_{ik}}{a_{kk}} of the pivot row from the rows below. Back substitution then solves from the last equation upwards.

The cost is about \frac{n^{3}}{3} multiplications.

Partial pivoting. Before eliminating column k, swap the row with the largest |a_{ik}| (i \geq k) into the pivot position. This avoids dividing by a zero or tiny pivot and keeps the multipliers |m| \leq 1, which controls round-off. Always use it on a computer.

Solve 2x + y − z = 8, −3x − y + 2z = −11, −2x + y + 2z = −3

Operations (with partial pivoting): swap R1 ↔ R2; m21 = -0.6667; m31 = 0.6667; swap R2 ↔ R3; m32 = 0.2000. The reduced upper-triangular augmented matrix is

| x | y | z | RHS |

|---|---|---|---|

| -3.0000 | -1.0000 | 2.0000 | -11.0000 |

| 0.0000 | 1.6667 | 0.6667 | 4.3333 |

| 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.2000 | -0.2000 |

Back substitution: z = - 0.2 / 0.2 = - 1 ;\ y = \frac{4.3333 - 0.6667 (- 1)}{1.6667} = 3 ;\ x = \frac{- 11 + 3 - 2 (- 1)}{- 3} = 2.

The solution is (x ,\ y ,\ z) = (2.0000 ,\ 3.0000 ,\ - 1.0000), which agrees with numpy.linalg.solve. Check in the first original equation: 2 (2) + 3 - (- 1) = 8 ✓.

Singular and inconsistent systems. If a zero pivot remains in a column after trying all rows below, the matrix is singular: either no solution (a row 0 = nonzero) or infinitely many (a row 0 = 0).

The determinant equals the product of the pivots times (−1) to the number of swaps.

4.2 Gauss–Jordan method and matrix inversion

Gauss–Jordan continues eliminating above the pivots too, reducing A to the identity; the right-hand side becomes the solution. Applied to the augmented matrix [A | I] it produces A^{-1}.

Inverse of [[2, 1], [5, 3]]

[A | I]: R_{1} \leftarrow \frac{R_{1}}{2} gives [1, 0.5 | 0.5 ,\ 0 ] ;\ R_{2} \leftarrow R_{2} - 5 R_{1} gives [0, 0.5 | - 2.5 ,\ 1 ] ;\ R_{2} \leftarrow 2 R_{2} gives [0, 1 | - 5 ,\ 2 ] ;\ R_{1} \leftarrow R_{1} - 0.5 R_{2} gives [1, 0 | 3, −1].

So A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 1 \\ - 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. Numerical check by NumPy: 3.0000, -1.0000, -5.0000, 2.0000 (row-wise).

Check A \cdot A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 5 & - 2 + 2 \\ 15 - 15 & - 5 + 6 \end{bmatrix} = I ✓.

Gauss–Jordan costs about \frac{n^{3}}{2}, more than Gauss elimination, so use it for inverses, not for single systems.

4.3 LU factorisation

If no row swaps are needed, A = L U with L unit-lower-triangular (1s on the diagonal, the multipliers below) and U upper-triangular (the result of elimination).

Then Ax = b becomes two cheap triangular solves: Ly = b (forward substitution), Ux = y (back substitution).

Once A is factorised, new right-hand sides cost only O (n^{2}), which is why LU is the workhorse of numerical libraries (with pivoting: P A = L U). The determinant is the product of U's diagonal.

Doolittle LU for A = [[2, 1, 1], [4, 3, 3], [8, 7, 9]], b = (4, 10, 24)

Elimination multipliers: m_{21} = 2 ,\ m_{31} = 4, then m_{32} = 3. So L = [ 1 ,\ 0 ,\ 0 ;\ 2 ,\ 1 ,\ 0 ;\ 4 ,\ 3, 1] and U = [ 2 ,\ 1 ,\ 1 ;\ 0 ,\ 1 ,\ 1 ;\ 0 ,\ 0, 2] (rows separated by semicolons).

Forward substitution Ly = b gives y = (4 ,\ 2 ,\ 2); back substitution Ux = y gives x = (1 ,\ 1 ,\ 1). The determinant is 2 \times 1 \times 2 = 4.

Check LU reproduces A and A x = b in code.

Variants: Crout (U has the unit diagonal), Cholesky A = L L^{T} for symmetric positive-definite matrices (half the work, no pivoting needed).

4.4 Iterative methods: Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel

For large sparse systems direct methods fill in zeros and cost too much. Iterative methods start from a guess and improve it. Solve equation \ast i \ast for x_{i}:

x_{i}^{(k+1)} = \frac{b_{i} - \sum_{j \neq i} a_{ij} x_{j}}{a_{ii}}

  • Jacobi: use only the old iterate x^{(k)} on the right (all components updated "simultaneously").
  • Gauss–Seidel: use the newest values as soon as they are available (components updated one after another), so it normally converges about twice as fast.

Convergence. Both converge for any start if A is strictly diagonally dominant (|a_{ii}| > \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}| in every row).

That is sufficient, not necessary; the exact condition is that the iteration matrix has spectral radius below 1. Rearranging the equations so that large coefficients lie on the diagonal often helps.

10x₁ − x₂ + 2x₃ = 6; −x₁ + 11x₂ − x₃ + 3x₄ = 25; 2x₁ − x₂ + 10x₃ − x₄ = −11; 3x₂ − x₃ + 8x₄ = 15, start 0

The matrix is strictly diagonally dominant (10 > 3 ,\ 11 > 5 ,\ 10 > 4 ,\ 8 > 4); the exact solution is (1.0000, 2.0000, -1.0000, 1.0000).

Jacobi (first six sweeps):

| k | x_{1} | x_{2} | x_{3} | x_{4} |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 0 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |

| 1 | 0.6000 | 2.2727 | -1.1000 | 1.8750 |

| 2 | 1.0473 | 1.7159 | -0.8052 | 0.8852 |

| 3 | 0.9326 | 2.0533 | -1.0493 | 1.1309 |

| 4 | 1.0152 | 1.9537 | -0.9681 | 0.9738 |

| 5 | 0.9890 | 2.0114 | -1.0103 | 1.0214 |

| 6 | 1.0032 | 1.9922 | -0.9945 | 0.9944 |

Gauss–Seidel (first six sweeps):

| k | x_{1} | x_{2} | x_{3} | x_{4} |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 0 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |

| 1 | 0.6000 | 2.3273 | -0.9873 | 0.8789 |

| 2 | 1.0302 | 2.0369 | -1.0145 | 0.9843 |

| 3 | 1.0066 | 2.0036 | -1.0025 | 0.9984 |

| 4 | 1.0009 | 2.0003 | -1.0003 | 0.9998 |

| 5 | 1.0001 | 2.0000 | -1.0000 | 1.0000 |

| 6 | 1.0000 | 2.0000 | -1.0000 | 1.0000 |

To get all components within 5 \times 10^{-5} of the exact answer Jacobi needs 12 sweeps and Gauss–Seidel 6.

The spectral radius of the iteration matrix is 0.4264 for Jacobi and 0.0898 for Gauss–Seidel; the smaller it is, the faster the convergence.

Because each sweep is cheap (n^{2} operations for a dense matrix, far less for sparse ones), iterative methods win for huge sparse systems.

Equation order matters

For x + 3 y = 5 ,\ 4 x + y = 6 (solution (1.1818, 1.2727)), Gauss–Seidel from (0, 0) gives (5.00 ,\ - 14.00) \to (47.00 ,\ - 182.00) \to (551 ,\ - 2198) \to (6599 ,\ - 26390): it diverges because the matrix is not diagonally dominant.

Writing the equations in the other order, 4 x + y = 6 first, gives (1.5000 ,\ 1.1667) \to (1.2083 ,\ 1.2639) \to (1.1840 ,\ 1.2720) \to (1.1820 ,\ 1.2727) \to (1.1818 ,\ 1.2727), which converges.

The two systems are mathematically identical.

4.5 Ill-conditioning

A system is ill-conditioned if tiny changes in A or b cause large changes in x. The culprit is a nearly singular matrix, and no algorithm can repair it; pivoting only avoids additional damage.

A nearly singular system

x + y = 2 ,\ x + 1.0001y = 2.0001 has the solution (1, 1). Change the right-hand side by 0.0001 to 2.0002: the solution jumps to (0, 2). A change of 0.005 % in one coefficient moved the answer by 100 %.

The two equations describe almost parallel lines, so their intersection point is very sensitive.

The condition number κ(A) = ‖A‖·‖A⁻¹‖ measures the amplification: relative error in x \leq \kappa (A) × relative error in the data.

For the matrix above \kappa = 40002, so a relative data error of 10^{-4} may produce a relative solution error of order one.

The 3 \times 3 Hilbert matrix, with entries \frac{1}{i + j - 1}, has \kappa = 524; it is moderately conditioned for n = 3 but becomes terrible as n grows. Rules of thumb: \kappa \approx 10^{k} loses about k significant digits.

Remedies: scaling, pivoting, higher precision, iterative refinement, or reformulating the problem.

4.6 Eigenvalues: the power method

The power method finds the dominant eigenvalue (largest in magnitude) \lambda_{1} and its eigenvector. Start with any v_{0} (with a component along the dominant eigenvector).

Repeat: w = A v_{k-1} ;\ \lambda_{k} = the entry of w with the largest magnitude; v_{k} = \frac{w}{\lambda_{k}}. Then \lambda_{k} \to \lambda_{1} and v_{k} → eigenvector, at a rate |\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}|.

A = [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −1, 2]], v₀ = (0, 1, 0)

| k | A \cdot v_{k-1} | \lambda_{k} (largest entry) | v_{k} (scaled) |

|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | (-1.0000, 2.0000, -1.0000) | 2.0000 | (-0.5000, 1.0000, -0.5000) |

| 2 | (-2.0000, 3.0000, -2.0000) | 3.0000 | (-0.6667, 1.0000, -0.6667) |

| 3 | (-2.3333, 3.3333, -2.3333) | 3.3333 | (-0.7000, 1.0000, -0.7000) |

| 4 | (-2.4000, 3.4000, -2.4000) | 3.4000 | (-0.7059, 1.0000, -0.7059) |

| 5 | (-2.4118, 3.4118, -2.4118) | 3.4118 | (-0.7069, 1.0000, -0.7069) |

| 6 | (-2.4138, 3.4138, -2.4138) | 3.4138 | (-0.7071, 1.0000, -0.7071) |

| 7 | (-2.4141, 3.4141, -2.4141) | 3.4141 | (-0.7071, 1.0000, -0.7071) |

The eigenvalue estimates climb towards 2 + \sqrt{2} = 3.4142, and the vector towards (- 0.7071 ,\ 1 ,\ - 0.7071) \propto \left( 1 ,\ - \sqrt{2} ,\ 1 \right).

The Rayleigh quotient \frac{v^{T} A v}{v^{T} v} of the final vector gives 3.4142, a faster-converging estimate. The smallest eigenvalue can be found by applying the method to A^{-1} (inverse iteration); shifts find the others.

4.7 Seeing the ideas: elimination, iteration speed and the geometry of ill-conditioning

Carl Friedrich Gauss gave elimination its name, and his portrait opens Plate 4.1. The plate also shows why some systems are dangerous: when two lines are nearly parallel, a tiny change moves their intersection a long way.

4.7.1 Eight uses of linear systems and their numerical solution

  1. Electrical networks. Kirchhoff's laws turn a circuit with many loops into a set of linear equations. A hydropower grid has thousands of nodes and is solved by computer. Elimination or iteration gives all currents at once.
  2. Structures and bridges. Engineers divide a truss or bridge into joints and write force-balance equations for each. The unknown forces in every member come from one big linear system. The same method checks buildings against earthquake loads.
  3. Economics and planning. Input-output tables describe how each industry uses the products of others. Solving a linear system shows how much each sector must produce to meet final demand. Governments use it in planning.
  4. Curve fitting. The normal equations of least squares are linear equations in the unknown coefficients. Every trend line and calibration uses them. A spreadsheet solves them in a moment.
  5. Computer graphics. Moving, rotating and projecting a 3D model involves solving linear systems for the transformation. Games solve millions of such equations per second. Graphics cards are built for it.
  6. Search and ranking. The ranking of web pages is an eigenvector problem solved by repeating a matrix multiplication, a method close to the power method. Recommendation systems use the same idea. Linear algebra runs behind the screen.
  7. Weather and flow simulation. Dividing the air or a river into small cells gives millions of linked equations, solved by fast iterative methods. Direct elimination would be far too slow. Choosing the right method decides whether a forecast arrives in time.
  8. Network and traffic analysis. Flow of traffic, water in a pipe network and data in a computer network follow balance equations. Solving them locates bottlenecks. Planners in Kathmandu can test a road change on paper first.

4.8 Pivoting, operation counts and tridiagonal systems

Why pivoting is not optional. Gauss elimination divides by the pivot a_{kk}. A tiny pivot makes the multipliers enormous, and the rounding errors they carry swamp the answer. Take

10^{-20}\,x + y = 1,\qquad x + y = 2 .

The true solution is x \approx 1, y \approx 1.

Without row exchange the multiplier is 10^{20}, the second equation becomes (1 - 10^{20})\,y = 2 - 10^{20}, and in double precision both sides round to -10^{20}, so y = 1 and then x = (1 - 1)/10^{-20} = \mathbf{0}: a completely wrong x.

Partial pivoting swaps rows so that the largest |a_{ik}| in the column (from row k down) becomes the pivot. Here the rows are exchanged, the multiplier is 10^{-20} and the computed solution is correct.

Scaled partial pivoting compares entries after dividing each row by its largest coefficient, which protects against badly scaled equations.

Cost of the methods. For an n \times n system:

Operation Multiplications (approx.) n = 10 n = 100 n = 1000
Gauss elimination or LU factorisation n^{3}/3 333 333 333 333 333 333
Forward and back substitution (one right-hand side) n^{2} 100 10 000 1 000 000
Gauss–Jordan, or finding A^{-1} about n^{3} 1 000 10^{6} 10^{9}
Cramer's rule with determinants by expansion about (n+1)! 4\times 10^{7} impossible impossible

Two lessons follow. LU is the right choice when the same matrix has many right-hand sides: factorise once for n^{3}/3 and each new b costs only n^{2}.

And one should almost never compute A^{-1} to solve Ax = b; it costs three times as much as elimination and is less accurate.

The Thomas algorithm (tridiagonal systems). Equations from splines (Section 2.6), differential equations (Unit 5) and the Laplace problem in one dimension have a tridiagonal matrix: nonzero entries only on the diagonal and its two neighbours, with sub-diagonal a_i, diagonal b_i, super-diagonal c_i.

Elimination then needs only two sweeps and about 8n operations in total, not n^{3}/3.

Forward sweep (i = 2, \dots, n): c'_1 = \dfrac{c_1}{b_1},\ d'_1 = \dfrac{d_1}{b_1}, and c'_i = \dfrac{c_i}{b_i - a_i c'_{i-1}},\ d'_i = \dfrac{d_i - a_i d'_{i-1}}{b_i - a_i c'_{i-1}}.

Back substitution x_n = d'_n, x_i = d'_i - c'_i x_{i+1}.

Five equations with 2 on the diagonal and −1 on both neighbours, right side (1, 0, 0, 0, 1)
i a_i b_i c_i d_i c'_i d'_i x_i
1 2 −1 1 −0.5000 0.5000 1
2 −1 2 −1 0 −0.6667 0.3333 1
3 −1 2 −1 0 −0.7500 0.2500 1
4 −1 2 −1 0 −0.8000 0.2000 1
5 −1 2 0 1 1.0000 1

The solution is x = (1, 1, 1, 1, 1), which a direct solver confirms. The algorithm is stable when the matrix is diagonally dominant (as here and in splines), and a system of a million unknowns takes a fraction of a second.

4.9 Cholesky factorisation for symmetric positive definite matrices

If A is symmetric (A = A^{T}) and positive definite (x^{T}Ax > 0 for every x \ne 0; equivalently all eigenvalues are positive, or all leading principal minors are positive), it can be factorised as A = LL^{T} with L lower triangular with a positive diagonal.

This needs only n^{3}/6 operations (half the cost of LU), no pivoting, and fails (a square root of a negative number) exactly when the matrix is not positive definite, so it doubles as a test for definiteness. The entries are

l_{jj} = \sqrt{a_{jj} - \sum_{k<j} l_{jk}^{2}},\qquad l_{ij} = \frac{1}{l_{jj}}\left(a_{ij} - \sum_{k<j} l_{ik}\,l_{jk}\right)\quad (i > j).

Cholesky factor of A = [[4, 12, −16], [12, 37, −43], [−16, −43, 98]]

Column 1: l_{11} = \sqrt{4} = 2, l_{21} = 12/2 = 6, l_{31} = -16/2 = -8. Column 2: l_{22} = \sqrt{37 - 36} = 1, l_{32} = (-43 - (-8)(6))/1 = 5. Column 3: l_{33} = \sqrt{98 - 64 - 25} = \sqrt{9} = 3.

L = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix},\qquad LL^{T} = A .

To solve Ax = b: forward-substitute Ly = b, then back-substitute L^{T}x = y.

Cholesky factorisation underlies least squares through the normal equations A^{T}A\,c = A^{T}y (the matrix is symmetric positive definite) and many statistical routines, although for ill-conditioned problems QR is safer (Section 2.13).

4.10 Norms, condition number and the meaning of a small residual

To say that one vector or matrix is "small" or that two are "close" we need a norm. For a vector: \|x\|_{1} = \sum |x_i|, \|x\|_{2} = \sqrt{\sum x_i^{2}}, \|x\|_{\infty} = \max |x_i|.

The matching matrix norms: \|A\|_{\infty} = \max_i \sum_j |a_{ij}| (largest absolute row sum) and \|A\|_{1} = largest absolute column sum. They satisfy \|Ax\| \le \|A\|\,\|x\|.

The condition number is \kappa(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|. It is at least 1 and measures how much the relative error of the data can be magnified in the solution:

\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \le \kappa(A)\,\frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}.

An almost singular system

\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1.0001 & 2.0001 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3.0002 \end{bmatrix}

has the solution x = y = 1. Change the second right-hand side by 10^{-4} (from 3.0002 to 3.0001) and the solution jumps to x = -1,\ y = 2.

Here \|A\|_{\infty} = 3.0002, A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -20001 & 20000 \\ 10001 & -10000 \end{bmatrix} with \|A^{-1}\|_{\infty} = 40001, so \kappa_{\infty}(A) = 3.0002 \times 40001 = 1.2\times 10^{5}.

The data error of 3\times 10^{-5} (relative) was magnified by about 10^{5}, in line with the bound. Rows that are nearly multiples of each other (the two lines are almost parallel) always give a large \kappa.

For comparison, the 3 \times 3 Hilbert matrix has \kappa_{\infty} = 748, the 5 \times 5 one 4.8\times 10^{5} (Section 2.13).

A rule of thumb: you lose about \log_{10}\kappa(A) correct digits of the solution, so with \kappa = 10^{5} and double precision you can trust about eleven digits, but with \kappa = 10^{15} none.

A small residual does not mean a small error. The residual of an approximate solution \hat{x} is r = b - A\hat{x} and the error is e = x - \hat{x}; they are related by e = A^{-1}r, so \|e\| \le \|A^{-1}\|\,\|r\|.

For the system above, take the poor guess \hat{x} = (2, 0.5): the residual is only (0, 5\times 10^{-5}) yet the error is (-1, 0.5). A tiny residual certifies an accurate answer only when \kappa is small.

Iterative refinement. After solving Ax = b in ordinary precision to get \hat{x}, compute the residual r = b - A\hat{x} (preferably in higher precision), solve A\,\delta = r with the same LU factors (cost n^{2}) and replace \hat{x} by \hat{x} + \delta.

A step or two removes the round-off error if \kappa(A) is not too large; if \kappa \gtrsim 1/\varepsilon the refinement cannot help.

4.11 Convergence of iterations and successive over-relaxation

When do Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel converge? Write the iteration as x^{(k+1)} = T x^{(k)} + c.

It converges for every start if and only if the spectral radius \rho(T) = \max|\lambda_i(T)| < 1, and the error shrinks by about \rho per iteration.

Strict diagonal dominance (|a_{ii}| > \sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}| for every row) is a convenient sufficient condition for both methods, but not necessary.

Spectral radii for the system 10x + y + z = 12, 2x + 10y + z = 13, 2x + 2y + 10z = 14

The iteration matrices have \rho_{\text{Jacobi}} = 0.2847 and \rho_{\text{Gauss-Seidel}} = 0.0447.

Gauss-Seidel therefore gains -\log_{10} 0.0447 = 1.35 digits per iteration, Jacobi only 0.55 digits, so Gauss-Seidel is about 2.5 times faster, which matches the tables of Section 4.4.

For the system x + 2y = 3,\ 3x + y = 4 (not diagonally dominant in this order) Jacobi has \rho = 2.449 > 1 and diverges, but exchanging the two equations to 3x + y = 4,\ x + 2y = 3 puts a dominant diagonal and makes it converge.

Successive over-relaxation (SOR). Gauss-Seidel computes a new value x_i^{\text{GS}} for each unknown. SOR overshoots in the direction of the change by a factor \omega:

x_i^{(k+1)} = (1 - \omega)\,x_i^{(k)} + \frac{\omega}{a_{ii}}\left(b_i - \sum_{j<i} a_{ij}\,x_j^{(k+1)} - \sum_{j>i} a_{ij}\,x_j^{(k)}\right),\qquad 0 < \omega < 2 .

\omega = 1 is Gauss-Seidel; 1 < \omega < 2 is over-relaxation and can be dramatically faster; the method diverges outside 0 < \omega < 2.

For symmetric positive definite tridiagonal matrices the optimum is \omega_{\text{opt}} = \dfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho_J^{2}}}, where \rho_J is the Jacobi spectral radius.

8 × 8 system with 2 on the diagonal and −1 beside it (right side all 1), stop when the change is below 10⁻⁶

Here \rho_J = 0.9397 and \omega_{\text{opt}} = 1.490. Iterations needed:

Method Iterations
Jacobi 216
Gauss–Seidel (\omega = 1) 115
SOR, \omega = 1.2 76
SOR, \omega = 1.4 45
SOR, \omega = 1.5 (near optimum) 26
SOR, \omega = 1.6 33
SOR, \omega = 1.8 72
SOR, \omega = 1.9 152

The right value of \omega cuts the work by a factor of 8 against Gauss-Seidel and 4 against Jacobi, but a value slightly too large costs much more than one slightly too small.

4.12 More on eigenvalues: Rayleigh quotient, inverse power method, Gershgorin and QR

Rayleigh quotient. For a symmetric matrix and a current vector x, the quotient \dfrac{x^{T}Ax}{x^{T}x} is a far better estimate of the dominant eigenvalue than the largest component of Ax used in Section 4.6: its error is of the second order in the error of x.

Power method on A = [[4, 1, 0], [1, 3, 1], [0, 1, 2]] from (1, 1, 1)

The true eigenvalues are 4.73205, 3 and 1.26795 (ratio 3/4.732 = 0.634, so the power method is slow). After the same iterations the two estimates are:

Step scale factor (largest component of Ax) Rayleigh quotient
1 5.0000 4.3333
4 4.8537 4.7170
6 4.7806 4.7296
8 4.7513 4.7317

After eight steps the scale factor is still off by 0.02 while the Rayleigh quotient is within 5\times 10^{-4} of 4.73205.

Inverse power method and shifts. Applying the power method to A^{-1} finds the eigenvalue of A nearest zero; applying it to (A - sI)^{-1} finds the eigenvalue nearest the shift s.

Each step solves (A - sI)\,y = x (factorise once, then reuse), takes x \leftarrow y/\max(y) and estimates \lambda \approx s + 1/\max(y).

Inverse power with shift s = 1.5 for the same matrix

Estimates of the eigenvalue after steps 1 to 5: 2.1429, 1.7442, 1.2602, 1.2690, 1.2678, converging to the eigenvalue 1.26795 nearest 1.5 and with the eigenvector (0.268, −0.732, 1).

A shift closer to the eigenvalue gives faster convergence; using the latest Rayleigh quotient as the shift gives cubic convergence for symmetric matrices.

Gershgorin's theorem. Every eigenvalue of A lies in at least one disc centred at a diagonal entry a_{ii} with radius r_i = \sum_{j \ne i}|a_{ij}| (the sum of the other absolute entries in the row).

For the matrix above the discs are centred at 4 (radius 1), 3 (radius 2) and 2 (radius 1), so every eigenvalue lies in [1, 5], and since the matrix is symmetric the eigenvalues are real.

This gives a free bracket for the power method and a free test for singularity: if no disc contains 0 the matrix is nonsingular.

The QR algorithm. All eigenvalues at once are found by the QR iteration used in library routines: factorise A_k = Q_kR_k and form A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k (a similarity transformation, so the eigenvalues are unchanged).

Under mild conditions A_k tends to an upper triangular matrix with the eigenvalues on the diagonal, largest first.

For the matrix above six unshifted steps give the diagonal 4.72815, 3.00387, 1.26798 (true values 4.73205, 3, 1.26795), with all off-diagonal entries below 0.09.

Practical codes first reduce A to tridiagonal (symmetric case) or Hessenberg form and use shifts so that the iteration converges in a few steps per eigenvalue.

Formula and fact sheet

  • Multiplier m_{ik} = \frac{a_{ik}}{a_{kk}}; partial pivoting: swap to the largest |a_{ik}| ;\ \det = \pm \Pi pivots.
  • Gauss–Jordan on [A | I] gives A^{-1}. LU: Ly = b then Ux = y.
  • Jacobi: old values; Gauss–Seidel: newest values; converge if diagonally dominant.
  • κ(A) = ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖; digits lost ≈ \log_{10} \kappa.
  • Power method: w = Av, λ = largest entry, v = \frac{w}{\lambda}; rate |\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}|.
  • Costs: LU n^3/3, substitution n^2, inverse \approx n^3; Thomas algorithm for tridiagonal \approx 8n; Cholesky A = LL^T costs n^3/6 (needs A symmetric positive definite).
  • \kappa(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|; \dfrac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \le \kappa\,\dfrac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}; digits lost \approx \log_{10}\kappa; \|A\|_\infty = largest row sum.
  • Iteration converges iff \rho(T) < 1; SOR: x_i \leftarrow (1-\omega)x_i + \omega\,x_i^{GS}, 0 < \omega < 2, \omega_{opt} = \dfrac{2}{1+\sqrt{1-\rho_J^2}}.
  • Rayleigh quotient \dfrac{x^TAx}{x^Tx}; inverse power with shift s: (A - sI)y = x, \lambda \approx s + 1/\max y; Gershgorin discs: centre a_{ii}, radius \sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|.

Chapter summary

  • Direct methods (Gauss, Gauss–Jordan, LU) give the exact answer in a fixed number of steps; use partial pivoting.
  • Iterative methods suit large sparse systems; Gauss–Seidel usually converges faster than Jacobi, and diagonal dominance guarantees it.
  • Ill-conditioned systems amplify data errors regardless of method; the condition number quantifies this.
  • The power method estimates the dominant eigenpair using repeated multiplication.
  • Pivoting prevents division by tiny numbers, the Thomas and Cholesky algorithms exploit structure, norms and the condition number quantify sensitivity (a small residual is not a small error), spectral radius governs iteration speed and SOR with a good \omega is several times faster than Gauss-Seidel; Rayleigh quotients, shifts, Gershgorin discs and QR extend the eigenvalue toolkit.

1. (x ,\ y ,\ z) = (2.0000 ,\ 3.0000 ,\ - 1.0000); the elimination is shown in Section 4.1.

2. A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 1 \\ - 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} (Section 4.2).

3. L = [1 ,\ 0 ,\ 0 ;\ 2 ,\ 1 ,\ 0 ;\ 4 ,\ 3 ,\ 1] ,\ U = [2 ,\ 1 ,\ 1 ;\ 0 ,\ 1 ,\ 1 ;\ 0 ,\ 0 ,\ 2] ,\ y = (4 ,\ 2 ,\ 2) ,\ x = (1 ,\ 1 ,\ 1).

4. From the tables in Section 4.4: after two sweeps Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel give the rows k = 2; Gauss–Seidel's x_{2} = 2.0369 is closer to the exact 2.0000 than Jacobi's value in its table row k = 2, because it uses the new values at once.

5. Strict diagonal dominance of rows: |a_{ii}| > \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}|. It is sufficient but not necessary; convergence actually requires the spectral radius of the iteration matrix to be < 1.

6. In the first order the matrix is not diagonally dominant (|1| < |3|) and the iteration matrix has spectral radius above 1; after swapping, the large entries 4 and 3 sit on the diagonal and the iteration contracts (compare the sequences in Section 4.4).

7. Small input changes cause large output changes, as in x + y = 2 ,\ x + 1.0001y = 2.0001 \to (1 ,\ 1), versus right side 2.0002 \to (0 ,\ 2). The condition number κ(A) = ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖ (here 40002) measures the amplification.

8. From the table in Section 4.6, the fourth iteration gives \lambda \approx 3.4000 (true 3.4142).

9. Plain elimination repeats the O (n^{3}) work for every new b. LU factorises once (O (n^{3})) and then each right-hand side costs only O (n^{2}) for the two triangular solves.

10. Without pivoting (pivot 0.0001): the multiplier is 10 000; row 2 becomes (1 - 10000)y = 2 - 10000, i.e. -10000\,y = -10000 in three digits, so y = 1.00 and x = (1 - 1.00)/0.0001 = 0.

The true solution is x = 1.0001,\ y = 0.9999, so x is completely wrong. With pivoting (swap rows): x + y = 2,\ 0.0001x + y = 1; the multiplier is 0.0001, y(1 - 0.0001) = 1 - 0.0002 gives y = 1.00 and x = 2 - 1.00 = 1.00, correct. Pivoting is right.

11. n^{3}/3 = 125000/3 \approx 41\,667 multiplications for the factorisation; each extra right-hand side costs one forward and one back substitution, n^{2} = 2500.

12. c'_1 = -0.5,\ d'_1 = 0.5; c'_2 = -1/(2 - 0.5) = -0.6667,\ d'_2 = (0 + 0.5)/1.5 = 0.3333; d'_3 = (1 + 0.3333)/(2 - 0.6667) = 1. Back substitution: x_3 = 1, x_2 = 0.3333 + 0.6667(1) = 1, x_1 = 0.5 + 0.5(1) = 1. Solution (1, 1, 1).

Q1 (5 marks). Solve 10 x + y + z = 12 ,\ 2 x + 10 y + z = 13 ,\ 2 x + 2 y + 10 z = 14 by Gauss elimination.

Augmented matrix. [10 1 1 | 12; 2 10 1 | 13; 2 2 10 | 14].

*Step 1 (pivot 10 ) . \ast m21 = \frac{2}{10} = 0.2 and m31 = 0.2: R2 = R2 - 0.2R1 gives [0 9.8 0.8 | 10.6]; R3 = R3 - 0.2R1 gives [0 1.8 9.8 | 11.6].

*Step 2 (pivot 9.8 ) . \ast m32 = 1.8 / 9.8 = 0.18367: R3 = R3 - 0.18367R2 gives [0 0 9.6531 | 9.6531] (Figure 4.1).

Back substitution. z = 9.6531 / 9.6531 = 1; y = \frac{10.6 - 0.8 x 1}{9.8} = 1; x = \frac{12 - 1 - 1}{10} = 1.

Q3 (10 marks). Compare direct and iterative methods for linear systems. Explain LU factorisation and ill-conditioning with an example.

Introduction. To solve Ax = b, direct methods (Gauss elimination, Gauss-Jordan, LU) give the answer after a fixed number of operations, while iterative methods (Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel) improve a guess until it is accurate enough.

Direct methods. Gauss elimination reduces A to upper-triangular form and back-substitutes, with cost about \frac{n^{3}}{3}.

LU factorisation writes A = L U with L lower triangular (holding the multipliers, here 0.2, 0.2, 0.18367) and U upper triangular (the reduced matrix).

To solve for any b, first solve Ly = b by forward substitution, then Ux = y by back substitution, each costing only n^{2}. LU is therefore ideal when the same matrix is used with many right-hand sides.

Gauss-Jordan continues to a diagonal form and can find an inverse but costs more.

Iterative methods. They store only the nonzero entries and need diagonal dominance (Figure 4.2). For a system with a million unknowns, such as a weather grid, they are the only practical choice.

Ill-conditioning. A system is ill-conditioned when small changes in the data cause large changes in the solution (Plate 4.1b).

Example x + y = 2 and x + 1.0001y = 2.0001 has the solution x = 1 ,\ y = 1. Changing the right side to 2.0002 gives y = 0.0002 / 0.0001 = 2 and x = 0: a change of 0.0001 in one datum changed the answer from (1, 1) to (0, 2).

The condition number is \mid |A| \mid x \mid |A^{- 1}| \mid = 2.0001 x 20,001, about 40,000, so relative errors in the data can be magnified up to 40,000 times.

Point Direct (LU) Iterative (Gauss-Seidel)
Answer after Fixed steps Until tolerance met
Cost \frac{n^{3}}{3} n^{2} per sweep, few sweeps
Memory Fills in zeros Keeps matrix sparse
Condition Works for any nonsingular A Needs diagonal dominance
Best for Small and medium systems Very large sparse systems

Conclusion. Use LU with partial pivoting for ordinary systems, iterative methods for huge sparse ones, and always check the condition number before trusting an answer.

Q4 (5 marks). Apply Gauss–Seidel and SOR with \omega = 1.25 to 4x - y = 3,\ -x + 4y = 3 (four sweeps from zero). Is over-relaxation always faster?

Formula. SOR: x^{(k+1)} = (1 - \omega)x^{(k)} + \dfrac{\omega}{4}\left(3 + y^{(k)}\right), y^{(k+1)} = (1 - \omega)y^{(k)} + \dfrac{\omega}{4}\left(3 + x^{(k+1)}\right); \omega = 1 is Gauss–Seidel. The exact solution is x = y = 1.

Sweep G–S x G–S y G–S max error SOR x SOR y SOR max error
1 0.750000 0.937500 2.5e-01 0.937500 1.230469 2.3e-01
2 0.984375 0.996094 1.6e-02 1.087646 0.969772 8.8e-02
3 0.999023 0.999756 9.8e-04 0.968642 0.997758 3.1e-02
4 0.999939 0.999985 6.1e-05 1.007139 1.002791 7.1e-03

Explanation. The Jacobi spectral radius is 0.25, so \omega_{\text{opt}} = 2/(1 + \sqrt{1 - 0.0625}) = 1.016, almost 1. Gauss–Seidel is already near the optimum, and \omega = 1.25 overshoots (the error changes sign each sweep).

Conclusion over-relaxation helps only when the system is slowly convergent (a spectral radius near 1, as in the 8 × 8 example of Section 4.11); choosing \omega carelessly can be worse than \omega = 1.
